sections.html:
Papillion is the Sarpy County seat and a southwest suburb of Omaha, so many residents work elsewhere in the metro area. It began as a railroad town in the 1870s, and Nebraska Highway 85 runs through downtown. The 2020 count was 24,159 residents.

The county seat status keeps the offices a seller needs close together. The Sarpy County Treasurer is at 1102 E. 1st Street, and City Hall is at 122 E. Third Street. That is a short list of stops for a homeowner who needs a tax receipt, a permit record or a copy of a recorded document before a sale.

Papillion stayed small for its first seventy years before growth took off: 1,034 people in 1950, 5,606 in 1970, 10,372 in 1990 and 24,159 in 2020. Much of the housing was probably built in the last five decades. If your house was built between the 1970s and the 1990s, buyers will want to know how old the roof, furnace, water heater and windows are.

Four streams shape local flood risk: Big Papillion Creek, West Papillion Creek, Walnut Creek and Midland Creek. The city's flood page says both Big and West Papillion Creek have a record of flooding.

  • August 1959: Big Papillion Creek flooded and six families were evacuated.
  • 1964: the largest flood of record on Big Papillion Creek killed seven people and caused about $5 million in damage, not counting personal property.
  • 1965: a second large flood followed.
  • 1993: heavy downpours damaged foundations and retaining walls in the Big Papio Creek watershed.

The Corps of Engineers built four dams in the watershed and levees have been added over time, but ongoing development leaves the creeks vulnerable to flash floods, especially if a levee fails.

sections.h2: Flood rules that affect a sale
sections.html:
If a house sits in a Special Flood Hazard Area, three things can affect a sale: lender insurance requirements, permits for any work, and a rule about large repairs. The city belongs to the National Flood Insurance Program and the Community Rating System, which may bring discounted premiums.

  • Flood damage is excluded from standard homeowners policies, and a separate flood policy waits 30 days before coverage begins.
  • A property's flood zone comes from the FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map, which lenders use and which the city's Planning Department uses for its overlay rules.
  • An elevation certificate shows whether a building is above or below the base flood elevation.
  • A Floodplain Development Permit is required before building, renovating or grading in the Special Flood Hazard Area.
  • If improvements or repairs cost 50 percent or more of the building's market value, the structure must meet new-building standards. For a house, that means the lowest floor, basement included, sits one foot above base flood elevation.

If you have flood damage and plan a major rebuild, ask the city about the 50 percent threshold before you spend money. Selling in current condition can be the simpler path.

Papillion has four distinct seasons, with about 30 inches of precipitation across a year and May the wettest month. The furnace works hard from December through February, the sump pump matters in spring, and freeze and thaw cycles wear exteriors. A buyer's inspector will test the sump pump, check the basement for moisture and look at grading around the foundation. If you have dealt with water before, keep the records ready.

Real estate taxes are paid in two installments. You can pay the Sarpy County Treasurer online, by mail to 1102 E. 1st Street, Papillion, NE 68046, through a secure dropbox outside the 1102 building, or in person at that address.

Payment or deadlineDate or rule
First half dueMarch 31
Second half dueJuly 31
Late interest14 percent a year under state law
Valuation protestJune 1 to June 30
Homestead exemption filingFebruary 1 through June 30 with the assessor

The assessment date is January 1 each year, and residential property is valued at or near 100 percent of actual value. Notices of changed value go out on or before June 1. Ask the Treasurer or your title company what is currently owed, so that nothing is left open on closing day.

The city's Building and Fire Safety department handles permits for residential and commercial building, mechanical, electrical and plumbing work, grading, stormwater management, signs and demolition. Applicants create an account on the online portal, then submit and pay there.

Deeds are recorded in Sarpy County. The grantor pays Nebraska's documentary stamp tax on deeds recorded July 18, 2026 or later, at $3.32 for each $1,000 of value or fraction. Gifts and estate transfers may be exempt, so check the state's list.

Papillion La Vista Community Schools serves the city and is a major local employer. Families relocating here often start with school attendance areas, so name the elementary school on your listing or offer summary. Boundaries can change, and we do not rate schools, so tell buyers to confirm the school for any address with the district before an offer is made.

The issues Papillion sellers raise are fairly consistent: a house near one of the creeks with flood insurance questions, a house that needs updating after decades of use, an inherited property no one in the family wants, or a move already on the calendar. Paying cash removes loan underwriting, so closing depends on title work, the deed and the Sarpy County recording steps. Request a written offer, weigh it against listing, and decline at no cost if it does not suit you.

sections.h2: Selling a Papillion house, step by step
sections.html:
1. Find out whether the house is in a mapped floodplain by checking the FEMA flood map or asking the Planning Department.
  2. Collect permit records, especially for decks, basements and additions.
  3. Ask the Treasurer or title company for the tax balance.
  4. Gather sump pump and basement moisture records if water has ever been an issue.
  5. Get a written offer and compare it with listing.
  6. At closing, the deed is recorded in Sarpy County and the stamp tax comes out of your proceeds.

If the house has flood damage and a rebuild would pass the 50 percent mark, the cost of meeting new-building standards may change the numbers. Ask the city first.

Because the city has a flood history and many houses date from the 1970s onward, buyers tend to ask three things: whether the house is in a Special Flood Hazard Area, whether the basement has had moisture, and how old the roof and furnace are. Prepare plain answers, with receipts where you have them. If the house is near Big Papillion Creek, West Papillion Creek, Walnut Creek or Midland Creek, say so up front and offer the flood map result for the address.

faqs.q: When are Sarpy County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due March 31 and the second half July 31. Pay the Sarpy County Treasurer online, by mail, in the secure dropbox or in person at 1102 E. 1st Street in Papillion. Late amounts carry 14 percent annual interest.

faqs.q: Is Papillion in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Parts of the city lie in mapped floodplains along Big Papillion Creek, West Papillion Creek, Walnut Creek and Midland Creek. Check the FEMA flood map for your address through the Sarpy County map service or the Planning Department, since a lender will require flood insurance for a mapped property.

faqs.q: What is the deed tax in Papillion?
faqs.a: The grantor pays $3.32 per $1,000 of value on deeds recorded July 18, 2026 or later, unless the transfer is exempt.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to repair flood damage in Papillion?
faqs.a: Yes if the property is in the Special Flood Hazard Area. A Floodplain Development Permit is required to build, renovate or grade there, and repairs costing 50 percent or more of the building's value trigger new-building standards.

faqs.q: When can I file a homestead exemption in Sarpy County?
faqs.a: Filing runs February 1 through June 30 with the assessor. The valuation protest window is June 1 to June 30.
